summary: Regional monthly iceberg density for a procedural generator. The SIZE classes are the published IIP scale (NOAA JetStream). The North Atlantic SEASON comes from IIP counts. Almost every DENSITY is an order-of-magnitude estimate, because no citable per-area iceberg density table was found. Read docs/environment/ICEBERGS.md before using these numbers.

units.density: bergs (small class and larger) per 10,000 km2 of open water, at the peak month
units.length_m: waterline length (longest side at the waterline), metres
units.height_m: height of the top above the waterline (freeboard), metres

confidence_scale.high: confirmed in a published or official source this session
confidence_scale.medium: well known or recalled; not re-checked this session
confidence_scale.estimate: derived or chosen by the author of this file; not a measurement

categories._note: Classes: the International Ice Patrol (IIP) scale as given by NOAA JetStream 'Icebergs' (https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/icebergs-max). Environment and Climate Change Canada MANICE (Manual of Standard Procedures for Observing and Reporting Ice Conditions, 9th ed. 2005), ch.1, uses a slightly different scale: medium 61-120 m, large 121-200 m, very large over 200 m long (the USCG NAVCEN Iceberg_Formation.pdf table gives the same 121-200 m). This file uses the IIP lengths throughout. Growler and bergy bit are the same in both. The US Coast Guard says no agreed scale exists outside the North Atlantic. 'tabular' here means a SMALL tabular berg below the Tournadre et al. (2016) 8 km2 limit; bigger ones are tracked one by one (US National Ice Center, NIC) and belong in ice.load_icebergs, not in this generator.

growler.source: IIP / NOAA JetStream 'Icebergs'; MANICE ch.1 (under 1 m high, about 20 m2)
growler.length_floor_note: 1 m lower length bound is an estimate (smaller pieces are brash ice)

bergy_bit.source: MANICE ch.1; WHOI sea-ice glossary (1 to under 5 m high, 100-300 m2)

medium.source: IIP scale, NOAA JetStream 'Icebergs' (16-45 m high, 61-122 m long). MANICE ch.1 (2005) gives 61-120 m.
medium.confidence: medium (not re-read this session; noaa.gov was blocked)

large.source: IIP scale, NOAA JetStream 'Icebergs' (46-75 m high, 123-213 m long, 401-670 ft). MANICE ch.1 (2005) gives 121-200 m.
large.confidence: medium (not re-read this session; noaa.gov was blocked)

very_large.source: IIP scale, NOAA JetStream 'Icebergs' (over 75 m high or over 213 m long; MANICE ch.1 2005 says over 200 m). The upper bounds (110 m, 450 m) are ESTIMATES to close the open class; the largest berg seen on the northern Grand Banks was about 320 m long and 10 Mt (Hibernia EIS, cited in Annals of Glaciology 'Icebergs: their physical dimensions').
very_large.confidence: medium (lower bounds; not re-read this session) / estimate (upper bounds)

tabular.source: Freeboard: Ross Ice Shelf front 15-50 m (USGS ROSETTA-Ice; J. Glaciol.). Length cap 2,800 m = side of an 8 km2 square, the Tournadre et al. 2016 (JGR Oceans 121:327-349) small-iceberg limit. Lower length 200 m: estimate.

bands_map._note: Mapping to the size bands of mno_env/ice.py BERG_BANDS (footprint, windage, lifetime). The ice.py bands are coarser game bands. 'giant' is never generated here.

draft_to_length.source: Annals of Glaciology, 'Icebergs: their physical dimensions and the presentation and application of measured data' (Labrador data 1973-78)

draft_max_m.source: Jakobshavn bergs 400-500 m, up to 600 m in older work (Enderlin et al. 2016, cited in The Cryosphere 17:371, 2023)

block_coefficient.applies: non-tabular bergs: volume = coefficient x length x width x (height + draft)
block_coefficient.source: estimate. With it a 120 m Labrador-type berg comes out near 0.7 Mt, between the Labrador median (about 0.39 Mt) and mean (about 2.2 Mt) in Annals of Glaciology Labrador statistics (OCR garbled, medium).

glacier_ice_density_kgm3.source: NOAA (about 11 % of a berg above water); ice about 900 kg/m3

shelf_ice_density_kgm3.source: BedMachine Antarctica hydrostatic density (Morlighem 2020, NSIDC-0756, doi:10.5067/E1QL9HFQ7A8M)

tabular_freeboard_fraction.source: derived: 1 - 917/1027 = 0.107 for solid ice; firn raises it (estimate)

wind_factor.source: About 2 % of the wind relative to the water (Garrett et al. 1985; Smith 1993). Bigg et al. 1997 use 1.6-1.8 %. Wagner, Dell and Eisenman 2017 (arXiv:1610.06403) show big keels follow the deeper current, so the tabular 1 % is an ESTIMATE.

melt._note: Martin and Adcroft 2010 (Ocean Modelling 34:111-124) form of the Bigg et al. 1997 (Cold Reg. Sci. Technol. 26:113-135) scheme. Coefficients are RECALLED from those papers and not re-checked this session (the research could not reach the PDFs).

wave_erosion.formula: Me = (1/12) Ss (1 + cos(pi A^3)) (Tw + 2)  m/day (sides), A = sea-ice fraction
wave_erosion.confidence: medium - verify; the NOAA repository paper noaa/49413 gives 0.5-1 m/day in calm water

max_life_days.source: Bigg et al. 1997: all model bergs melted within about 5 years, most in year 1. Grounded giants live longer (A-23A calved in 1986 and stayed grounded in the southern Weddell Sea until 2020, about 3 decades) but are not generated here.
max_life_days.confidence: medium - verify (Bigg et al. 1997, Cold Reg. Sci. Technol. 26:113, not read this session)

growlers_per_berg.source: estimate. IIP counts leave growlers out; berg break-up and wave erosion shed many pieces. Break-up into small bergs is about 80 % of the mass loss of large Antarctic bergs and basal melt about 18 % (Tournadre, Bouhier, Girard-Ardhuin and Remy 2015, large-berg fragmentation study, J. Glaciol.; not re-read this session). Small bergs are mainly produced by break-up of large ones (Tournadre et al. 2016, JGR Oceans 121:327-349).

mix.source: estimate. Shares of bergs (small and larger). No published class shares were found. Antarctic bergs are mostly tabular when they calve; the generated small and medium Antarctic bergs stand for break-up pieces.

crossings_48n_monthly.source: Feb-Jul: IIP 2024 North Atlantic Iceberg Summary, mean bergs crossing 48N, 1983-2024 (Feb 22, Mar 121, Apr 191, May 209, Jun 115, Jul 41; year about 715). Aug-Jan: ESTIMATE, spreading the remaining 16 of 715 over those months. TO DO: Table 1 of IIP_2024_North_Atlantic_Iceberg_Summary.pdf (navcen.uscg.gov) gives every month Oct-Sep; put its Aug-Jan means here. navcen.uscg.gov was blocked in this session and in the research session, so neither the Feb-Jul values nor the table were re-read.
crossings_48n_monthly.confidence: medium (Feb-Jul; from the research session, not re-read) / estimate (Aug-Jan)

long_term_mean_1900_2018.source: IIP 2019 Annual Report; data NSIDC G10028 doi:10.7265/z6e8-3027. The IIP 2018 report already gives 492 for 1900-2017, so the 1900-2018 value may be 492-495: check against G10028 (nsidc.org was blocked in this session). For context: the 1983-2014 mean is 787 (IIP reports).

residence_months_south_of_48n.source: estimate. Small bergs on the Grand Banks lose up to a third of their mass in a day; bergs reaching the Banks have already lost about 85 % of their mass (ECCC 'Iceberg melt').

grand_banks_water_km2.source: derived: water area of the two grand_banks boxes below (1,496,945 + 216,350 km2 on 0.1-degree cells with the mno_env.geo Natural Earth land mask), rounded to 1,000 km2. The model spreads the IIP count evenly over these boxes, so the divisor must be their area. (An earlier version divided by 500,000 km2, an estimate of the area inside the IIP limit of all known ice, and then filled the whole 1.74 million km2 box: about 3.5 times too many bergs.)

regions.name: Grand Banks and south of 48N (IIP area)
regions.source: density = IIP crossings x residence / box water area (see 'iip'); peak about 0.6 per 10,000 km2 in May (209 x 0.5 = about 105 bergs in the boxes). Boxes are a rough cover of the IIP limit of all known ice (estimate). North of 46.5N the west edge is 57.5W, so Cabot Strait and the Gulf of St Lawrence are left out. Current: Labrador Current branch along the east edge of the Banks, 0.1-0.5 m/s (general oceanography, estimate).

regions.name: Labrador Sea shelf and NE Newfoundland
regions.source: estimate, inside the 1-10 per 10,000 km2 order the research gives for the Newfoundland approach. Season: spring peak ahead of the IIP 48N crossings (estimate). Current: Labrador Current, estimate. Boxes: the second box stops at 57.5W so the Gulf of St Lawrence (west of the Strait of Belle Isle) gets no modelled bergs; few enter it (estimate).

regions.name: Baffin Bay and Davis Strait
regions.source: estimate. West Greenland outlet glaciers (Jakobshavn and others) are the main Northern Hemisphere source; bergs stay frozen into the pack in winter. Current: Baffin Current south on the west side, West Greenland Current north on the east side; net proxy is an estimate. Boxes: Baffin Bay and Davis Strait proper. Foxe Basin (65-70N, 73-80W; no tidewater glacier source, not a known iceberg area) and Hudson Strait (west of 64.5W) are left out; Hudson Strait is the next region.

regions.name: Hudson Strait and Frobisher Bay
regions.source: ESTIMATE, a tenth of Baffin Bay: some Baffin Current bergs enter the eastern strait and Frobisher Bay; no local source. No density source found. Season copied from Baffin Bay (estimate). No current proxy (zero).

regions.name: East Greenland and Denmark Strait
regions.source: estimate. Sources include 79N glacier (tongue about 70-80 km, The Cryosphere 17:2851, 2023) and the SE Greenland fjords. Current: East Greenland Current south along the shelf, estimate. Boxes: the East Greenland shelf and Denmark Strait only (west of 25W south of 67N, west of 15W north of it). The bergs stay mainly on the Greenland shelf and round Cape Farewell; bergs off south and east Iceland are rare, so those waters have no modelled bergs (estimate; no density source found east of about 25W).

regions.name: Canadian Arctic Archipelago and Nares Strait
regions.source: estimate. Few bergs: Ellesmere ice-shelf fragments (shelves 535 km2 by 2015, ECCC; about 455 km2 after the July 2020 Milne loss of about 80 km2, ESTIMATE by subtraction) and Petermann pieces (2010 berg about 250-275 km2: 253 +/- 17 km2, Falkner et al. 2011, Eos 92(14); 275 km2, Luckman and Floricioiu, EGU2011-10857) in Nares Strait. No current proxy (unknown, zero). Boxes leave out 68-70N east of 87W, so the north end of Foxe Basin gets no bergs.

regions.name: Barents Sea and Svalbard
regions.source: estimate inside the 0.1-1 per 10,000 km2 order from the research. Sources: Svalbard, Franz Josef Land, Novaya Zemlya; the only consistent record is Abramov 1996 (atlas 1881-1993, 100 x 100 km cells), not read. Statoil: 2.6e-5 encounters per year for a 100 m target at Skrugard (Eik et al., POAC 2023). Season shape and current are unknown (estimate, zero). South edge 74N: the berg limit lies far north of the Norwegian coast. Keghouche et al. 2010 (J. Geophys. Res. Oceans, doi:10.1029/2010JC006165) model the southern limit moving seasonally around 74-76N in the west; about 20 bergs on the Finnmark coast in spring 1929 are cited as exceptional (Vinje and Kvambekk 1991, Polar Research); a 2018 berg at 75.12N 19.13E is called among the southernmost (POAC19-058). None of the three was re-read this session.

regions.name: South-east Barents Sea (Shtokman area)
regions.source: ESTIMATE, a third of the northern Barents value. Bergs from Novaya Zemlya and Franz Josef Land reach further south in the east than in the west (Keghouche et al. 2010, doi:10.1029/2010JC006165, not re-read). No density source found.

regions.name: Kara Sea and Franz Josef Land
regions.source: estimate (as Barents). Abramov 1996 atlas is the source to read.

regions.name: South Georgia and Scotia Sea
regions.source: estimate. Over 90 % of Antarctic bergs enter the Weddell Gyre and drift north to South Georgia (NASA Earth Observatory, BAS; popular source). Over 50 % of small-berg volume is in the South Atlantic (Tournadre et al. 2016). No season found: flat. Current: Antarctic Circumpolar Current, estimate.

regions.name: Weddell Sea outflow and Iceberg Alley
regions.source: estimate inside the 1-10 per 10,000 km2 order from the research ('iceberg alley' east of the Antarctic Peninsula). Current: Weddell Gyre northward along the Peninsula, estimate.

regions.name: Amundsen and Bellingshausen Seas
regions.source: estimate. Sources include Pine Island (B-49, 2020, about 300-350 km2, NASA EO) and Getz. Current: Antarctic Coastal Current westward, estimate.

regions.name: Ross Sea
regions.source: estimate. Ross front about 600 km long (USGS); B-15 calved here in March 2000. Current: westward coastal flow and the Ross Gyre, estimate.

regions.name: East Antarctic coast
regions.source: estimate. Bergs from Amery, Shackleton, West and other shelves ride the westward Antarctic Coastal Current (estimate).

regions.name: Southern Ocean, South Atlantic sector
regions.source: estimate. Tournadre et al. 2016: over 50 % of small-berg ice volume is in the South Atlantic; each basin has a probability maximum. ALTIBERG (CERSAT/Ifremer) monthly fields should replace this once read.

regions.name: Southern Ocean, other sectors
regions.source: estimate (an order below the South Atlantic, after Tournadre et al. 2016).

zero_elsewhere.source: No region outside the list above has a modelled iceberg density. This leaves out rare historical strays (for example Antarctic bergs seen near 35S, and North Atlantic bergs well south of the IIP area in extreme years).

radar_calm_nm.source: Growler 0.5 nm or not at all on conventional radar (Canadian Coast Guard ice hazard radar paper, high). Bergy bit under 1 nm conventional; enhanced: bergy bit beyond 4 nm, growler beyond 2 nm (sigma S6 vendor brochure, medium; CCG trial: beyond 3 nm). Bergs 2-9 nm for a low antenna (BoatUS, low). Small-to-tabular values are ESTIMATES; the range used is also capped by the radar horizon.

radar_sea_state_factor.source: ESTIMATE following the rule of thumb that small ice is lost in clutter from about sea state 3-4 (CCG paper; IIP 1940s study: heavier seas mask even medium bergs). Growler echoes are comparable to sea clutter (Radar and ARPA Manual).

visual_day_cap_nm.source: estimate. Bergs larger than a bergy bit are limited by visibility and the geographic horizon only.

visual_night_factor.source: estimate for a moonless night (no source found)

geographic_range_coefficient.source: Bowditch, American Practical Navigator, 2019 ed., Vol. 1, Appendix B / Table 12: distance to the horizon D = 1.17 sqrt(h_ft) = 2.07 sqrt(h_m) nm (standard refraction)
geographic_range_coefficient.confidence: medium (formula well known; the 2019 text was not re-read this session)

sonar_false_contact_index.source: DESIGN INDEX, not a probability. No citable false-contact rates or iceberg target strengths were found. The ice face is a strong reflector (impedance estimate R about 0.4, about -8 dB, derived). It rises with keel depth.

breakup_source_level_db.reference: dB rms re 1 uPa at 1 m
breakup_source_level_db.source: Dziak et al. 2013, Oceanography 26(2) (iceberg A53a break-up)
